title: Van Leer Log Cabin
description:
Originally on Irish road, now in the Conestoga school sports fields.  Restored 1960

On 1820 tax roll owned by Alexander Torbert.  Sale recorded in 1857. The cabin is a rough log house used by a tenant or son before he came into his inheritance.  Originally log walls inside and out.  Could have been a kitchen or shed for a grander house.  German style log cabin of a kind built in the 18th century, but built after 1800 in remembrance of earlier architecture.  Machine-made nails used in cabin, which were not available until after 1800.

title: Reading Election Returns, Paoli Inn, 1832
description: Joshua Evans was born in Paoli, Pennsylvania. He was a hotel keeper and also engaged in agricultural pursuits. He married Lydia Davis 29 February 1808. He served as a member of the Pennsylvania House of Representatives in 1820. He was appointed the first postmaster of Paoli on December 9, 1826, and served until February 13, 1830. He was the president of the Tredyffrin Township, Pennsylvania, school board from 1836 to 1846. He served as brigadier general of the State militia.Evans was elected as a Jacksonian to the Twenty-first and Twenty-second Congresses. He was not a candidate for renomination in 1832. He resumed his former business pursuits and died in Paoli in 1846. Interment in the cemetery of the Great Valley Baptist Church in New Centerville, Pennsylvania.from Wikipedia

On Valley Creek just south of route 23.  Dam built around 1790 to replace the dam destroyed by the British.  Dam pulled down by Valley Forge State Park in 1920 (newspaper reports). - Mike Bertram

Also a postcard dated 3/13/1920 to T.L. Eyre.  Note with postcard: There is no merit in the assertion that the dam in question is of continental value, in that it is alleged to have furnished power to grind flour for use of Genl. Washington and soldiers.  There was no dam there at that time, and we know as a matter of history, that this fable recently inventer, is without foundation.  In fact 1st dam at mouth of gorge, the present location, was built 1812

title: Diagram of railroad track at (New) Centerville
description:
Attached is a copy of a sketch I found at Hagley outlining the trackage at Centreville, circa 1899. The sketch was part of a file relating to a proposal to build three coal bins for a Mr. S. Whitworth, who was also the coal dealer at Cedar Hollow. The bins were actually built. (Rick Bates)

Some other info I've found - The track scale and scale office was built in 1875. The water tank may have been built the same year, although I'm not sure of this; my only evidence is a reference to an agreement for a water supply with an Isaac Walker, dated in 1875. In 1876, $657 was spent to build a retaining wall at Centreville. The station name was officially changed from CENTREVILLE to NEW CENTERVILLE effective November 28, 1910.Here's more regarding the water tank. In 1953, it was deemed that a water supply was no longer needed and the water rights were sold to a Warren M. Wells of Devon for $500 so that he could use it for a swimming pool on his property. He was also to pay $9.00 per year for an encroachment of a 258-ft pipeline on railroad property. The memo outlining this deal stated that the water rights had been acquired over a number of years between 1853 and 1921 and that a reservoir and pipeline had once been in use, but that the water tank and related facilities were already dismantled.

title: Espenshade's Wayside Inn
description:
Business Card.  Note on Back: The highest development of the Wayside Inn was reached when Lancaster Turnpike became the chief highway and model roadbed in the United States.  It led from Philadelphia to Lancaster, 62 miles long, and was commenced in 1792 and finished in 1794. (Continued in Notes)

The road replaced the old Conestoga or King's Road, having at that time nine toll bars between Philadelphia and Lancaster.   For the benefit of the drovers, travelers and teamsters the inns had signs painted, descriptive of their names, such as Black Bear, Spread Eagle, General Warren, and the General Jackson, which is now the Wayside Inn.  The General Jackson has had many owners and also names, being built by the Evans family in 1763, and was known as a lodge stand, having a room kept specially for the meetings of the Farmer's Lodge, No. 182, of the Free and Accepted Masons, who met here from 1822 until 1830.   This Inn was considered the fifth outstanding inn between Philadelphia and Lancaster.  In one of its cellars is the brick vault where barrels of ale were kept.   Being closed a few years at the beginning of the Second World War, the Inn was bought and opened July 17th by the Espenshade sisters and renamed Espenshade's Wayside Inn.  It is known in many states, with a reputation of cleanliness and good food.   The Inn is Located 18 miles from Philadelphia on Route No. 30.Book 6

title: Traveler's Rest Tree, Waterloo Avenue, Berwyn
description:
The Centuries-old, ungainly white oak tree located on the west side of Waterloo Avenue near the foot of Waters' hill, about half a mile south of Berwyn, toppled over on Sunday night, March 24 1996, a victim of rotten roots and old age.  Known locally at 'Traveler's Rest,' it was so named according to tradition, because it was halfway between Valley Forge and Media and often used by early travelers as a stopping place. (Continued in Notes)

The tree was an historic William Penn oak estimated to be 300 or more years old according to the book 'Penn's Woods 1682 - 1982' by Halfred Wertz and Joy Callender.  It stood on the property of Donald and Mary Kane (the old Waters place of the late 1800s).  Its trunk had a circumference of 17 feet, 2 inches, measured at a 4.5 foot height, and was estimated to weigh 9 tons from roots to crotch.Book 6

title: Valley Forge c. 1790 dam
description:
Note on card: Mar.13, 1920 to T.L. Eyre: There is no merit in the assertion that the dam in question is of continental value, in that it is alleged to have furnished power to grind flour for the use of Genl. Washington and soldiers.  There was no dam there at that time, and we know as a matter of history, that this fable recently inventer (sic), is without foundation.  In fact 1st dam at mouth of the gorge, the present location, was built in 1812 - 1814, about 36 years after evacuation of V.F.  This dam erected in 1814 was to furnish power for a small cotton mill, which incident had not the least connection or association with the encampment at V.F. - Richard L. Jones

It is more likely that this dam was originally erected in 1790 when the new forge was first taxed. - Mike BertramBook 6
